utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'm informed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you would like to address the Chamber. I already can tell you that if it's urgent we'll listen to it now. On the other hand, we'd like, if possible, to finish with Dr. Vilicic, so if it's a matter that could wait for a second then please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is urgent but it will be brief. First thing, copies of tapes, we would just like to have it on the record that we perhaps were not able to ask certain questions of expert Vilicic. I say perhaps because it's not sure because practically when the copies were -- when the copies were made, and this is not a reproach, the time that elapsed, we were not able to do what we wanted to do during the examination-in-chief. That is when we were asking our questions, that is the first point. The second point, Mr. President, and this is very important, when I say it's urgent we think that it should be dealt with straight away to do with the decision that was passed yesterday by the presiding judge of Trial Chamber I, unless I'm miss taken in relation to the issue that we asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I take it, just an order to have matters clear. Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the case is the withdrawal -- this was to do with the lacuna in the law directly communicated to the Appeals Chamber and today we find ourselves in a specific situation, the following: The withdrawal was requested, the cases before the Appeals Chamber and in this type of situations there is a quasi-legal lacuna received by the judge who passed the decision in question. Now, this is to do with a domestic jurisdiction that when such a situation is presented, that is, when there is a withdrawal, that is, when it is to the level of the appeals authority or the text itself, what happens is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The Defence would like to request that the proceedings will be stayed as long as the Appeals Chamber is dealing with the matter of the accusation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially since you refer to many legal systems, this is an important legal matter, I would say, which is very much to be dealt with in written form. So if there are any submissions to be made, I mean today or these three hours will not considerably change --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the reason why I'm intervening now is following the observation of the Judge and his order so that the Defence is not reproached with a belated request to do with the suspension. Now, we are intervening immediately just to in limine litis on this point and if you tell us that we can formulate that in writing at a later date we will do that but from this very moment we have formulated it. The -- our position is suspension of all procedure and if we continue to question this witness and others, this is -- we're taking this with a reserve so that our position is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear that you object against the continuation of the proceedings at this very moment. When I said it's something for written submissions, especially because you referred to systems of law and that of course is not something that could be explained easily just by orally informing us but precise sources would be needed to better study your argument. When you say the later date, of course the matter is such that the Defence should do that as soon as possible and not just leave it too long so that we have your argument, written argument, available, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is there any other issue to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I have some issues to raise but I heard you say earlier that you preferred to complete the evidence of this witness unless it's urgent. The matters that I have are not so urgent so perhaps I could make my points at a later time during the day if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that would be possible if there is a later time today available for us because we have to leave this courtroom at exactly quarter to 2.00. I have a few decisions and observations. The Defence has asked for more time for the examination of the expert witness Radinovic, the Chamber initially granted three hours then the Chamber granted four hours; both four hours for the Defence and four hours for the Prosecution. The Chamber will consider, depending on how the parties proceed in the examination and cross-examination to add one hour to those four hours for both parties and it will depend on the efficiency the parties demonstrate during examination of the expert witness. There has been another issue which needs some attention and that is whether there would be any breaks and how to deal with rebuttal evidence if there is any request for rebuttal evidence. Of the Prosecution should indicate as soon as possible from now on whether they want to present rebuttal evidence. They should specify what rebuttal evidence they would use unless, upon good cause shown, the Chamber would decide that for a specific part of the rebuttal evidence you have in mind that you would not have to provide further details as to what statements, what witnesses, et cetera, but in general, we are at such a stage of the proceedings that the Prosecution is in a position to disclose to the Defence what it intends to seek - this is not a decision of the Chamber that it will be admitted - so that the Defence can start preparing for the cross-examination of rebuttal witnesses and again if there's any specific reason or a specific subject why it would unfair -- why it would be unfair to the Prosecution to present this data, the Prosecution can apply for an exception. The final list of the final request of rebuttal evidence, because there might come up new things, you never know, should be filed immediately after the close of the Defence case, on that same day immediately. The Chamber then will take presumably four days to hear the other party on that request and give a decision. It can be expected that the Chamber will give an indication of rebuttal evidence that will be admissible right after the hearing of the other party even if it's not a complete decision yet on the request as a whole, but if there are elements on which we can decide immediately, we'll do that so that the Prosecution is in the position to further prepare for calling that evidence. That would also mean that we'll start with the presentation of rebuttal evidence if any is required not certainly -- certainly not later than five working days after the close of the Defence case. So we'll have a break of presumably four, perhaps five days. The same procedure will apply as far as evidence in rejoinder is concerned, that means that after the close of the rebuttal evidence, the Defence should immediately file whether they want to present any further evidence. We'll then also take four to a maximum five days to hear the Prosecution on that request. We'll also give a decision as soon as possible so that the Defence can prepare for travel arrangement for witnesses, if necessary. The parties should be aware that the rebuttal evidence and evidence in rejoinder is presumed not to take much time and certainly not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. more than five days. You should stay well within these limits, of course as far as the Chamber can oversee now because we are giving a decision not knowing exactly what the parties will request but this is just as guidance to the parties. If that is -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. I should indicate that the issues that I will be raising a.m. Some stage during the date are likely to take in the order of 20 minutes and in my respectful submission, it would be appropriate for the Trial Chamber to hear these matters today rather than Monday because some of them concern the witness Radinovic and incidentally, Mr. President, I think you said Radovanovic, I expect you meant Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. We've received further correspondence from the Defence this morning which concerns us greatly about his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So I would be grateful if, Mr. President, it would be possible to indicate a time that I could return and raise these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. During the first break, I'll try to get more information on whether there would be a possibility to deal with that matter perhaps later during the day because we really would like to finish with Professor Vilicic. That does not mean that if we would not meet in this courtroom before a quarter to 2.00 that the matter could not be discussed in whatever way by the parties, it's a practical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: One of the matters, Mr. President, should be on the record, and it doesn't concern Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It might be that we find another courtroom. I still have to investigate how to deal with it and that's -- may I also make clear that the parties should really work as efficiently as possible with the expert witness Vilicic and I already can announce that the Chamber has quite some questions for Professor Vilicic. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Just to allow everyone to save time, the Defence and I'm speaking here about Ms. Pilipovic, is offering to Mr. Ierace to have a meeting if there are any problems to do with this witness. It could be this weekend, it could be Sunday to shed some light on these problems, so we can resolve everything, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever can be resolved between the parties is to be preferred and let's -- the Chamber is still optimistic about the potential of the parties to resolve their own problems. Madam usher, could you please escort Professor Vilicic into the courtroom. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you understand English, Professor Vilicic, I don't have to say dobradan, but just good morning may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stamp, please proceed. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just so we have an idea how much time does the Prosecution have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just -- Madam Registrar is computing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before my time begins to run, Mr. President, may I just ask how much there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar is just -- total time used until now is three hours and three quarters of an hour that would leave another one hour and 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like to return to the Markale incident. At page 53 of your report, you determined the drop angle from the record on measurements of the traces, the mechanical damage to the ground and you used the formula that was published by Dr. Vukasinovic to measure the angle of descent or all of you used it. In that paragraph, you used the figures 26 centimetres and 56 centimetres. Were those numbers taken from the report of the crime analysts who examined the crater?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Dr. Vukasinovic's theory or formula proceeds on the basis that if the angle of descent of a falling shell forms an angle of less than 90 degrees to the horizontal surface of the ground, the peripheral star-shaped and elliptical traces of the damage to the ground around the crater are more distinct and longer on the side of the crater than the shell came from and he applied mathematical procedures to that premise.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Again, I don't think that you understood. Vukasinovic here is looking at the trace of the front part of the projectile, that is, of the frontal ogival part. During the explosion it forms two circles, one circle which is around the fuse and the other which is going from the frontal part of the projectile. What is probably confusing for you that there is no the back trace which is logically, depending on the direction where the projectile came from the fragments of the other part of the projectile, from the central part towards the stabiliser, those fragments create that trace in the -- going in the direction of where the projectile come from. This has probably caused confusion for you because this frontal part AO is longer than OB. I think you can see that the drawing is made in such a way that you can see it on the sketch that the projectile came from the direction where the trace is lesser but that has nothing to do with the other part of the trace which appears when the projectile hits the ground. I can show you this in a better way when you see the picture at the very beginning of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is whether or not if the shell impacts at an angle of less than 90 degrees on a horizontal surface of the ground, the traces would be longer and more pronounced in the direction from which a shell came, and I think you've answered the question. That's all I wanted to ask you. Indeed, Doctor, although you have used the mathematical formula in the Markale case, any expert artillery officer can look at a crater and from the mechanical damages, from the splash marks of the fragments on the ground, I'm on to a different question, the question is this: That any artillery expert could look at the splash marks on the ground and come to an assessment of angle of descent on the basis of the dimensions of the splash mark. And as a matter of fact, you have done so in respect to incident one. At incident one at page 31 --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, every artillery expert can give a rough assessment of the direction just like us. We were also not able to assess precisely the direction of fire. We have just done so approximately, and if it's necessary, I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get to explanations in due course. So Doctor, the -- are you aware of the evidence of Professor Zecevic that when he measured the crater, he found that the drop angle was just about 60, it was between 55 and 65 so that is basically in agreement with the results of your mathematical methodology? You have to answer verbally, you just nodded.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were two other UNPROFOR personnel from a specially-organised team of experts who measured the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that a number of UNPROFOR members assessed the drop angle in the direction in the UNPROFOR report that I have with me here, you can see that they checked this on three occasions. After the on-site investigation that was carried out by the SJB, the public security centre and then the following on-site investigation carried out by Zecevic and at that time the crater had already been changed. I listened to the testimony of Zecevic here. I heard how he determined the drop angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just answer the questions. I understand that you disagree with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the methodology but you have agreed with me that the results of Zecevic's methodology basically corresponds with yours. What I'd like to ask you now if you are aware that the UNPROFOR members of that special team that measured the angle of descent found it to be in a range of 950 to 1.100 mils, which corresponds to 53 to 61 degrees. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that John Hamill Brendan -- I know that eight measurements were taken from those various data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Efforts to measure the angle of descent correspond and they were independent of each other.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I am looking to see what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause before asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they didn't translate to me what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay, we can agree -- I'm just finding some points of agreement quickly. We can agree that the measurements of the angle of descent, yours, Zecevic's and the UNPROFOR experts correspond between 53 to 65 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that in the report, that we have here, we stated that the best examination was carried out by the team led by Professor Zecevic. It was the most complete report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... All part of the analyses, yours, Zecevic's UNPROFOR, all the angles correspond. Generally speaking would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with Zecevic's but not with UNPROFOR's because they are very different. And it's true that UNPROFOR determined itself on the basis of those measurements because the crater was so damaged that they were not in a position they weren't able to do it precisely and some of them didn't do it at all. Out of the eight, on three occasions, I think I can even remember this, I think it was on the 11th of August, the -- sorry, the 11th, 15th or 16th of February 1994 I have it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last question on this point. I suggest to you that the two members of the UNPROFOR team who measured it had the same results as yourself and Zecevic. What document is that, please?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the UNPROFOR report on explosion at the market in Markale dated 5 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you consulted to answer my question. I am simply trying to get the points of agreement you will agree that all persons who measured the crater, you using your scientific methodology that was published by Dr. Vukasinovic, Zecevic, by placing the fin back in the hole although you don't agree with that methodology, and the UNPROFOR members came to the same conclusion. That is all I want you to answer in respect to angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't confirm that like that because if you have a look at the results reached by UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR didn't determine the same angles. I had to have a look at it because they are given in mils, not in degrees; it's between 950 to 1.400. Share that with 16.7 and you will obtain the angle, divide that by 16.7. I didn't do that, I didn't divide it because UNPROFOR claims here that these results are not exact, are not reliable and -- I apologise. Because the measurements were made on a crater which was significantly damaged in relation to the initial state of the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Vilicic, you have reviewed all the findings just mentioned by Mr. Stamp, I take it. Is any of these findings in contradiction with the drop angle you calculated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes. Captain Verdy on the 5th of February, Verdy his measurement was greater than 83 degrees, Russell took a measurement and it was more than -- just a minute, Russell measured 71 for the low one up to 1.300, 71 to 77 degrees, Hamill made measurements and it was 950 shared with 16 -- divided by 16.7, Hamill was close to that result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that last one contradicting? 950.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. No. That one corresponds to the figure, that's why I said that only Mr. Hamill, Hamill's results corresponded to Zecevic's results and to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking. So Captain Verdy is the one who is in contradiction with your calculation, and the other one was Russell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [interpretation] Major Russell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Other contradiction in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the angle, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is no other contradiction, is there?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't. That's why I said not all of them, that some and I emphasized the fact that Hamill's results were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And may I just indicate to you for future reference, I asked you about the members of the UNPROFOR team of experts. Captain Verdi and Major Russell were not members of that team although their results were recorded here. The two members of the team were Major Hannes [phoen] And Commander Hamill who did results. So what I want to ask you now, doctor, is it agreed also that a 120 millimetre shell will only lodge in the ground if it is fired on charge 3 and above; is that agreed?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even with the first charge, it will lodge in the ground if it's been translated correctly. No, no, that's not correct. Each charge results in the projectile lodging in the ground but if the charge is greater, it penetrates to a greater depth and if the charge is smaller, it penetrates to a lesser depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to object here because either we're talking about Markale and then it involves the Markale surface or it's a general question and then we have soft surfaces, hard surfaces et cetera so the question is not sufficiently precise, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The way in which the question was put is whether it could lodge at all on whatever surface if it would land -- if it would have been fired at a certain charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The thing is in the report, so I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Stamp, I ask you, you were talking about a projectile lodging in the ground, did you refer to the tail fin or to the projectile because that caused the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, if the transcript has it correctly I thought I referred to the tail stabiliser fin, but maybe I could just rephrase the question and it's in the report at page 53, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor, at 0 plus 3 or greater charges -- withdrawn. If a 120 millimetre mortar is fired and has a drop angle of 53 to 65 degrees and it is fired from charges 0 plus 3 or greater, what would be the range, according to your knowledge of the range tables?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the initial angle for the drop angle if that's what interests you if it's between 55 and 65 degrees since I assume that that's what you are referring to. For that drop angle, the range should then be greater than 5.700 from ten metres, if it has five charges. If it has three charges, then it would be from 3.900 metres and with six charges, 6.500 metres, 6.444 according to the fire tables because these are drop angles from a minimum of 55 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those would be the maximum ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, within that angle of descent, or for that angle of descent at charges 3 and higher, what would be the minimum distance?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to 3.700, if the drop angle was 85 degrees with three charges. You asked me what the minimum ranges are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The drop angle is not 85 degrees. I'm asking for a drop angle between 55 and 65 degrees. For charge 3, what is the minimum distance? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three charges, it could be about 4.000 metres. With five charges about 5.000 metres and with six charges, 6.400 metres these are the maximum ranges. The minimum ranges -- please allow me. I don't have a complete firing table here I only have a graphic firing table here. With three charges, the drop angle could be small. If we increased the number of charges, the drop angle has to be greater because the velocity is greater. You asked me whether it was for four, five, or six charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Time on this question. I'm asking you now at angle -- drop angle of 55 to 65 degrees, what is the minimum range for the 120 millimetre mortar fired at charge 3, 0 plus 3?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to be precise but if the drop angle remains constant, you have to increase the initial elevation. The same drop angle with one charge if you have the same drop angle in one charge, you can't fire from different ranges. One drop angle and one charge corresponds to one range. Another drop angle and another charge corresponds to a different kind of range but if you have an angle of 55, even if you use six charges, two or three charges, you can't obtain this; do you understand? The rule for the trajectories, curvature of trajectories is still applicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the last time, 120 millimetre on charge 3 angle of descent 55 to 65 degrees, what's the minimum range, in your estimation? If you can't give me that precisely, give me an estimated figure?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need a minute or two to obtain this angle from the graphic table. Your Honour, can I show you this on the ELMO? This is the table -- these are the tables for the 120 millimetre shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that assists you in giving an answer to the question, please put it on the ELMO so that we can see it and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the third charge, this is the line for the third charge. The drop angle for the third charge is here for the maximum range. To answer your question, I have to increase this angle so that it's an angle of 55 or 65 degrees and then by turning this around, I'll tell you what the exact range is. Very roughly, I can tell you but it's a matter of improvisation, the angle has to be 55 degrees. The rule for rotating the trajectory, if you put the compass here, turn this line, rotate the line, I get a range of about 3.000 metres according to these graphic tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, doctor, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I should have a full firing table, the complete firing tables in order to answer this question, the complete firing tables for 120 millimetre mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you are aware that a shell impacting in Markale market from a direction of 18 to 23 degrees -- I beg your pardon from a direction of 18 degrees and travelling a distance a minimum of 3.000 metres would have been fired from deep within Serbian-controlled territory; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because in the report, it states everything, there's the assumption that the projectile came from that direction so that it's impossible to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Just some premises, some assumptions, assume they are true, just some assumptions and apply your expertise to your opinion. The simple question: In the north-east, 18 degrees to the north, at a distance of 3.000 metres from Markale market and beyond, you are within Serb-controlled territory; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but according to the statement, the demarcation line is about 2.500 metres in that direction, I think. One of the officers in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp has limited time so you answered the question by the first yes, and if Mr. Stamp would need further explanation, he'll certainly ask for it. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I suggest for the record that the confrontation line in that direction was approximately --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Vilicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, I said 2.200, I didn't say 3.000 metres. I said 2.200 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever, that's where the confrontation lines are is not specifically something an expert in ballistics would know as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So Doctor, for the time being, just please focus on my questions. Please. What you have done in your report, Doctor, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp, I would like to ask something. When you say that you said 2.200 metres and not 3.000 metres, you are referring to the range or to the distance of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the documents that are here, this is the distance that I saw, the demarcation line, according to an UNPROFOR officer was 2.200 metres in that direction. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, Doctor, I suggest to you that it is having regard to these obvious and agreed upon truths that we just went through that the mortar shell must have come from deep within Serb territory, that you have raised this issue of penetration depth by using a Sandia study to suggest that the incident did not occur as alleged. Do you agree or disagree, it's a yes or no --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, because the translations are not adequate, the translations of your questions. Our entire study is based on analysing the impact location. We didn't analyse the demarcation line, et cetera. Our main task was to determine the projectile used and attempt to determine, on the basis of the effects of that device, to try and determine whether it was possible for such a projectile to be used and our conclusion was that this was not correct and you are insisting on these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In your report, in your report, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but you base your conclusions that it was not possible in this report that you prepared on the -- your use of the Sandia study. May I just read page 54 your report the third to last line, "This analysis," referring to your report, "Uses the latest results in testing the penetration of natural obstacles and concrete conducted at the Sandia National Laboratories in the United States." And having analysed the findings using the Sandia results, you conclude that the Sandia study proves that from what the evidence at Markale indicates that there is no known mortar of such ballistics and you make that conclusion at page 56.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the case of concrete. In the case of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you bring your source with you, the Sandia study? Do you have it with you now in your attache case?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, I didn't bring it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you object if I -- maybe I could ask the Court if -- I will just proceed, I'm sorry. I have a copy of the report from the Sandia National Laboratories which I propose to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First thing, as usual, as it happens, can we please have the Serb version; yes or no? Yes or no? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether there's a Serbian translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document is a document which is used in the Defence study it is the basis of their report. We are entitled to take it that the Defence has their own resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. It's not a problem. I thought you were referring to an additional document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record this is document P3801.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Sandia National Lab, Professor -- Professor, Professor, I'm not asking you to read the report or to look at it as you have read it and used it for your report. Usher, could you please take the document. Thank you very much. The Sandia National Lab, Professor, is considered generally and clearly by you to be the leading researchers in the penetration of projectiles into various materials. I'm awaiting an answer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Is it question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And they are --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you the address thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In their latest work, "Penetration Equations", are there limitation for the conditions for these equations to apply?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you please, do you have the report, the Sandia report 980978, there are two reports here, not just one. [In English] "Simplify a analytical model for penetration for lateral loading," Sandia 980978.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are there any limitations, that's a question, for the application of the Sandia study?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For this case, no, the one I mentioned, no, but let me just tell you Vukasinovic did exactly this, he personally did this calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you do the calculation, do you understand the calculation? Doctor, please just answer my question, did you or did you not, time goes?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am prepared to show you, yes, yes, yes, I can show you the calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is one question asked in this tone, asking the Professor if he understands a calculation. I'm afraid that is really rather rude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I notice that there is some irritation. I'm not going to give you my observations as what caused it but may I ask you, Professor Vilicic, to strictly limit your answers to what you have been asked and Mr. Stamp, the more gentle you ask something, the better the chance you get the answer you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I apologise to the Court and to the witness. I never mean to be impolite, it's just that I'm trying to press along as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I please -- Mr. -- If there is any need to consult it should be done at such a level of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, would you please wait until the Defence has had the opportunity to consult with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order not to waste time, what we will do at the end, which I hope will come soon, at the end of the cross-examination by Mr. Stamp we will need to confer for a few moments. These are difficult technical questions to do with General Galic and we really need to confer. If you will allow us, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at page 6 of the study? Did you use those equations there, equations 3.1 and 3.2? Perhaps it would be easier if we look at appendix 2, the authors have changed the figures in appendix 2 to the metric system just for clarification, in the early part of the document, at page number V the report is written in U.S. units but in the nomenclature in appendix A they are written in international units. Did you use these equations, equations A 3.1?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have it back on 3.1, please? This calculation, this formula does not correspond to our formula. These are given in the English system of measurements so these coefficients that are mentioned here do not correspond to the metric system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you looking at appendix 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just -- you turn back now to page 5, didn't you, Professor Vilicic, you're looking at page 5? Could we just look on the ELMO what page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You will find the equivalent in continental measures on page A2. That is the first appendix, appendix A, second page. There you find the values expressed in the metric system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That formula, yes, A-3.2, that's the one that we used, 3.2. That's the one that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: LP is D. For the velocity of penetration higher than 61 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. They have two formulas, one for velocity higher than 61 metres and one for velocity lower than 61 metres and you used the formula for velocities equal to or lower than 61 metres per second which is A-3.2, I understand you to be saying that.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Higher than 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, there is a modification to the equations for lightweight penetrators and I'd like you to have a look at your report at page 54 in English or without doing that, tell us which modification you used?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did it according to the formula 3.2, 3.2, the formula 3.2 calculation from the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me read immediately below 3.2, "The modifications to the equations for lightweight penetrators are," and they give for soil and soft target and for rock and concrete targets. Now, was the modification you used for the mortar 2 stabiliser fin, being a lightweight projectile, the modification at A-3.4? You can look at your report.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: KX is this value here, A-3.4 formula, KX.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you used the modification for concrete and for hard targets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for a clarification. Professor Vilicic, you said you applied equation A-3.4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's E-3.4 because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please point at it? Would you please point at which one you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This KX 0.46 times H 0.15 but that's irrelevant if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not asking for an explanation at this moment. I'm just asking when you applied, you say it's A-3.4. I do read on that line that M is equal to or higher than 182 kilograms. Stands M for the mass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's what it says here, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used an equation for a mass of over 182 kilograms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one coefficient KX is 0.46, it's not a calculation, it's just a coefficient, it's a value, a formula for the coefficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand but doesn't it say just above that the equations have to be adapted in one way or another for lightweight and perhaps also for heavyweight objects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A-3.3, could you point at it? Yes. Doesn't it say that that would apply if the mass is less than 27 kilograms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a mistake. This is our mistake but we made this mistake in a sense that we get a lower result than we would get with this other formula because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just stop you. Are you telling us that you made a mistake but you did that in order to get a more favorable result from your calculation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A more favorable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More favorable to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this, you get a favorable, more favorable result in terms of length of penetration because if we had applied this coefficient we would have had, as a result, a shorter length of penetration. May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, you are telling us that it would not harm the Prosecution's case since it would only be better for them, the equation you used. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, please note that the modification you use also is for rock as is written in the middle of the page and concrete, in brackets hard targets. Now, overall, the equation, the Sandia equations are there limitations on the conditions of use for these equations and when I say overall, are there guidelines in which you are told that in some situations they are not to be used?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably exist but you want me to know all the documents from A to Z and I don't have this document on me. Please, Your Honours, may I just say something, Your Honours, may I just say something very briefly? So far, I have always stated that what we've used as a basis for obtaining results, we used Berezansky formula which gives the deepest length of penetration and it is according to the Berezansky formula which gives higher results for the length of penetration compared to the Sandia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained that. You have explained that the Berezansky formula is the most favorable one for the Prosecutor's case. You said that at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at page 5 of the study, section 3 which introduces a study. And you will see at the sixth line, the following are assumptions or limitations which apply to all the penetration equations. And you will see at number seven below, the minimum penetrator weight about five pounds for soil, ten pounds for rock, concrete, ice, and frozen soil. They give the mass in international units in the appendices. Five pounds being two kilograms, and ten pounds being five kilograms. What is the weight, the mass of a stabiliser fin that you have recorded in your report at page 55, I'm sorry, could you look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if five pounds are two kilograms but ten pounds cannot be five kilograms but four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the most difficult part of the mathematics we deal with these days, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you are quite correct, Your Honour, but I'm referring to the figures used by the scientists in the appendix.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the mass of a stabiliser fin, isn't it 1.2 kilograms?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minimum, minimum 1.2. Average.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The size you used, according to your report in the equation was 1.2 kilograms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in all the calculations according to all methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a scientist, giving an expert report to a Court, wherein that report you say you rely on a particular study and analysis to form a conclusion that an incident as important as Markale is a hoax, couldn't have happened, wouldn't it be prudent to indicate to the Court all of the situations in which you have applied the study outside of its own limitations and conditions? In other words, you have given us a lot of mathematical figures in your equations, shouldn't you have told the Court about these figures and give an explanation why you did not abide by the researchers and scientists at the Sandia National Lab?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, first of all, what you are insisting on insisting to discredit me as a scientist, I'd like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not doing that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second thing, before this Chamber, before this Chamber I have said, stated from the beginning, and I'm saying and stating this now, what I suggest, if this is possible, according to the least favorable Berezansky formula we can assess the events on the Markale market and you can see, you will see that Berezansky formula confirms this, Sandia formula is not the basis. We have also quoted the Sandia laboratory but it gives lower results for the length of penetration compared to the Berezansky's formula.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We will get to the Berezansky formula later. You can rely upon that. But you use a Sandia report in the document that you have written, prepared yourself and given to the Court and that is why I'm asking questions about it. I don't know if this is an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I think it would be an appropriate time for a break. You would have half an hour left approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would have half an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would respectfully apply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would more efficiently put your questions to the witness, it could be done in approximately half that time, Mr. Stamp. Clear questions give clear answers and as you noticed, whenever the witness goes on paths you did not invite him to go on, the Chamber interferes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The problem is it appears sometimes impolite and it to some extent text interrupts the work of the interpreters if I interrupt him every time he goes off on a tangent and that is -- there is a huge mass of material which the Court should be at least brought to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, we'll consider the matter but please keep in mind that according to our calculations you have 35 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, I will try to proceed as efficiently as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the witness is called into court, may I indicate to the Court that having regard to the time that has been indicated, there would be quite a variety of matters which this Court ought to be aware of, matters involving the fuse, the components of a fuse which is a very important consideration, the fragments from 120 millimetre mortar, the issue of the absence of 82 millimetre mortar stabiliser fins which the expert in his report has used to draw conclusions, and some other conclusions that he has drawn in respect to other incidents need to be explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, I do understand, Mr. Stamp. On the other hand, the Defence was given such time, I mean sometimes it can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be really done far more quickly so please start and we'll see where we end but as a starting point, you've got 38 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's another thing that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I do not agree, I see that the Defence took a little bit over the five and a half hours granted, they used as a matter of fact, five hours and 46 minutes, that would then add to your 38 minutes remaining another 16 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 52. I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, makes 54 minutes. Otherwise you will have to prioritise. We might not be able to go into every single detail of every part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, could you have a look at page 54 of your report, I'm sorry, page 55 of the English version of your report.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And look at the penultimate line in which I will say the values of the coefficient KS is 0.9.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the S, the KS factor is the factor that relates to the resistance of the target material or the surface to penetration?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two co-efficients S and K.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you use 0.9?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have a look at the body of page 11 of the Sandia study at page 11. You are aware that the Sandia institute is a military research laboratory and when they speak of concrete and hard material, they include reinforced concrete.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the middle of page 11, there is a sentence, and I'll read it, "In those cases where insufficient data exists to permit calculating the S number for concrete, a default value of S equals 0.9 is recommended." And that is the one you used. Please answer verbally, orally?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's correct. That's the value.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would it also give assistance in the S number for soil in the section beginning on the same page, going over into page 12?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For soil, yes, but I don't know what that has to do with concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They recommended among these S numbers 8 to 10 for soil fill material with the S number range depending on compaction. You see that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For S it says from 15 to 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see in the middle of page 4.2 on page 12 where it recommends an S number of 8 to 10 for soil fill material with a S number range depending on compaction?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, various values are given here for S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in our case, it would be between 2 and 4, that would be more or less what Borko Zecevic said the ground at Markale was such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly you did not use 2 to 4 you used 0.9, secondly the evidence is that the dirt under the asphalt --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For concrete, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At Markale, I suggest to you, that the evidence is --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we took the value of 0.9 for concrete, concrete isn't soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you that by using the S factor of 0.9 for concrete and applying that to the Markale situation where there was soil and the recommended S factor is 8 to 10 depending on the compaction of the soil is effectively reducing ten-fold the depth that you would arrive at in your calculations.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. First of all, the ground wasn't soil, it wasn't compact soil. The first time we heard what kind of ground it was was from Zecevic. It says clearly that it was macadam, expert Higgs said macadam. I said also that unfortunately Markale was covered and that it wasn't possible to determine with precision what was beneath the asphalt. In any event, on the photographs, in the photographs, you can see small stones, there was stone down below.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... First of all you say you weren't able to determine with precision the condition of the surface. I'd like you to have a look at the Sandia report, very quickly, please at page -- if I could find this quickly, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, what was the composition of the surface, in your view, according to Professor Zecevic? What did he say about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zecevic said that it was a macadam surface and Higgs said that. Macadam, in English, is tarmac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please listen to me very carefully. I only asked Zecevic. How thick was the asphalt layer, according to Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say exactly, two to three centimetres, I don't know, I'd have to have a look. I haven't remembered that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will read to you, that's perhaps useful for your next answers, that Professor Zecevic said, "There was a layer of asphalt probably two centimetres thick and the underneath there was sand and small rocks, gravel, small stones." Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for future reference, the UNPROFOR report, there was a force engineer with that type of specialty who said that below the asphalt it was soil and pebbles, that is written in the report by Sergeant Jeff Dubon [phoen]. You said that you did not have precise information, Doctor, about the quality of the surface. Have a look at page 13 of the Sandia study quickly, please. Page 13. Section 5 speaks about the accuracy of the equations and it says, it is virtually impossible to differentiate between the accuracy of the penetration equations and the accuracy of the S number," and the S number is what applies, the surface. If you are using these equations, and as you have said you did not know what the surface was about, should you not have advised the recipients of your report about this accuracy factor? Do you think it would have been prudent to have noted in your report the accuracy issues?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It also says that when the term for a lightweight penetrators is applicable, which you -- I'll just read. You said -- not you, the report indicates that when the term for lightweight penetrators --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, plead read out slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The report indicates that when "a term for a lightweight penetrators is applicable, KH, KS, the inaccuracy is likely to be greater." It also says that the "equation for the S number for a rock has an inaccuracy of 20 per cent when the data is very good to as much as 100 per cent when the data especially the Q value is little more than a guess." Do you think it would have been prudent to indicate that there was these considerations that would have applied to the use of the equation?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the value, the -- at the moment, I think that we should have mentioned everything relevant so that the Trial Chamber could have all the information, but it doesn't make -- it doesn't introduce any significant changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just ask you whether a 100 per cent deviation would not make a significant change to the outcome of the equation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an error of 100 per cent is still such that it would not have an effect on our conclusions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you -- I mean it would have an effect on the numeric outcome of your calculations I take it, but I do understand that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you take it that it would not make any change to the conclusion as to whether, in this particular case of the Markale market whether the projectile would have been fired from one side of the confrontation line or from the other side; is that right, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wouldn't have changed the conclusion that the stabiliser, the normal mortar shell can penetrate to such a depth in the ground, regardless of the fact that we didn't know, given the information that we had, certain factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do we not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we didn't know with were precision what the nature of the ground was in order to use the nature of the ground you need to use a special procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you and try to better understand your testimony. I understood your testimony to be that for a tail fin to be embedded in the ground at a depth of 20 to 25 centimetres that it could never have landed there, on the basis of your calculations, it could never have been embedded there as a result of firing that the projectile by a 120 millimetre mortar. So your calculations exclude for the possibility --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such a depth of penetration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you say that we have some uncertainties about the exact composition of the soil but whatever that would be, you could exclude even if that K value would be -- well let's say significantly deviant from the one you used; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for the Sandia National Laboratory equations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then perhaps put a few questions to you in this respect in order to clarify the issue and could I perhaps ask you to follow me in a few assumptions. Madam usher, could you please put this document on the ELMO for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have also prepared some sketches that relate to the explanations I'd like to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please look at this sketch? It represents more or less in the sketch what is the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution's case is that it is alleged that the mortar was fired somewhere from the hills in -- near the area of Mrkovici and landed on the Markale market. So what I'm now trying to find out together with you, whether your calculations would exclude for certain that this could be true even if there was a deviation of the K value of 100 per cent, as you said. I'll try to explain what I did write down on this sketch, and please correct me immediately if there's any specific reason that I'm wrong. I took, as a matter of fact, the speed, the velocity at firing for a high charge, that would be 0 plus 6 that would cause a speed of 322 metres per second at firing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would result, as far as I understood your calculations, you were so friendly to make on my request, at a velocity of impact of 258 metres per second if the shell would land at an altitude of 500 metres less than the altitude on which it was fired. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, upon explosion, the tail fin would be pushed back at a speed of 154 metres per second, according to your report, if I understood it well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would then be the speed at the start of the penetration of the tail fin in the soil? What would be the velocity of that tail fin? Am I correct if I calculate that at 104 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for asking this question. Mr. President, I will show you on the sketch what the velocity would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would just like you to answer my questions and then you get full opportunity to explain whatever you want. I am just trying to verify whether my understanding of your report and of your tables is a correct one. If there's any need to explain anything else, please do so after we have finished this exercise. What would be the speed at the start of penetration? I would calculate that at 258 metres per second minus 154 which makes 104 metres per second; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you did not. 154 metres per second is the velocity of the ejection of the stabiliser because of the effect of the gases, propellant gases. And it's not in correlation with the initial velocity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No I'm not saying that it is in relation. Please listen to me carefully. I started on the assumption of a shell being fired at a certain speed which produces a speed, a velocity at arrival at a level of 500 metres lower which is related to the velocity of firing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have an unrelated factor to that and that is that the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference of velocity is 104 metre per second, that's what you said. That is not the velocity that the stabiliser is going at when it is penetrating, it is lower and let me explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please explain where I did not understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the shell exploded instantaneously at the very surface, there would be no penetration and you saw from the tables that the shell, although the fuse will function, it will penetrate. Here, I have made a diagram. At the moment of the impact, the projectile has this velocity that you've put 258 metre per second. The projectile goes for a while through this trajectory when the fuse functions. At the moment when the projectile explodes, then it stops, the velocity is zero. The stabiliser follows the projectile trajectory until the moment of the explosion and it has the velocity of the projectile itself because the projectile, as it is penetrating, it is reducing its speed. Let us assume that at the moment when the projectile exploded, it had the velocity of zero but now, since the stabiliser got detached from the projectile, it still has the inertia that we are following. Now, what is the velocity of the stabiliser at that moment? It has this value here, you see, proportional to the length of penetration. From that moment, this is when we calculate the velocity of the stabiliser and how it continues to penetrate into the soil, into the surface so I've already mentioned this several times. We took the least favorable case that the shell disappeared at the moments when it impacted the surface so there was no penetration of the shell itself. The stabiliser has the velocity that you have mentioned, 104 metres a second. It will have the highest possible penetration. With this realistic velocity stabiliser has less of a penetration that is why we state that when you add up the depth of penetration of the shell up to the explosion and the continuation of the penetration of the stabiliser together with the velocity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you just allow me to reread the last part of your answer so that ... So you do agree that once the stabiliser has separated from the exploded body of the shell, it has a speed of 104 metres per second; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we took the least favorable -- the stabiliser has the velocity that you have mentioned, 104 metres a second, that is when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Please read everything. Do I understand you well that the stabiliser loses some of its velocity because the shell, the front end of the shell penetrates the soil for a very short while before it explodes so we would have to deduct from the 104 metres per second first the decelerating effect the resistance of the soil on the front end of the shell up until the moment of explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do I find this exactly in your report? Because as far as I can see, on page -- would you please look with me on page 56 of your report. You have there added the velocity needed to penetrate for 18 centimetres in the ground and you have added the 154 metres per second. Let's then, at this very moment, forget about the decelerating effect of the first small moment of impact and let's go a different way. We'll come back to this point later, I'm not forgetting about it. Could you please take in front of you the table you gave as an extra which reads, "Comparison the penetration of stabiliser of a mortar shell in concrete and" -- no, I'm using the wrong one. You gave the new one with the yellow lines in it where you calculated. Yes. Could we start with an impact penetration of 20 centimetres just as for calculation reasons. If the 20 centimetres would be 2 centimetres of asphalt and 18 centimetres of soil, ground and stone, what would be needed to -- what velocity would be needed to embed at such a depth in the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Higher than 114.4. It will be slightly higher. That would depend on the quality of the asphalt, whether it was old or new, old asphalt is softer than new asphalt,.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The other way around, the other way around, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 116, 117, well let's just assume, slightly over because the first two centimetres are asphalt and not ground. Okay. Now, if that would be needed for penetration of 20 centimetres, using the addition you used on page 56 of your report, what would have been needed as velocity at the start of penetration, that is 116 and I see that you add then 154 because that's the power that pushes back, at least the effect of the power of the detonation that pushes back. That would be 154 and that would be how much together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be over -- let me have a look at the table plus 114, that would be 268, around 270 metres if we take into consideration the asphalt as well or a lesser depth of penetration if we eliminate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether Professor Zecevic, when he measured 20 to 25 centimetres, what he exactly measured? Did he measure up until the surface of the market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall exactly. I was present during his testimony. What he explained that he said he measured two depths, that is there was a hole and he mentioned two depths and I think he said 2 to 240 millimetres, 20 to 24 centimetres, I think I have the data somewhere exactly. JUDGE ORIE. [Previous translation continues] ... Said that 200 millimetres to 250 millimetres he said between 20 centimetres and 24 centimetres. Next question: Do you know how he measured that? Did he measure that under the angle or did he use the height as you took it for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that Professor Zecevic said that when he placed the stabiliser inside, he took a protractor to check the slope and he saw that it was somewhere between 20 and 30 degrees and on the basis of that angle, in this way he measured the angle of descent would be between 60 and 70 degrees, I remember that's what he said and he also mentioned these two values. You corrected me, I thought it was 20 to 24 you said 20 to 25 centimetres but I don't think that he explained in detail as far as I can recall of course, I have notes that I took during his testimony so I don't know exactly, I don't know exactly the measurements or rather how, the method that he used to make those measurements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we do not know whether he took the measure diagonally or that he, as a matter of fact, reduced what he measured to the vertical depth, the, as you call it, H? We do not know exactly whether he used LP or H; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two points. I know that he said he measured two points, probably that this 20 was the nearer point and 25 was the further point but as far as I understood, the stabiliser that's 44 centimetres diameter but really if it's a question of a tunnel, if really the stabilisers remained embedded in this tunnel, if this tunnel remained the way that the stabiliser fell in, he probably measured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That's a different matter. He explained 20 centimetres, 25 centimetres, one point to the next point. If the tail fin was embedded in the ground, and if he would have projected the depth he measured to the vertical standard, would, at an angle of approximately 60 centimetres, would that create a difference of 5 centimetres? You understand what I mean, otherwise I'll ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You need the diameter of the tail fin, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no -- it's the sine of the angle. That will be the depth for 25 centimetres and if you did it like this then it would be 21.5. If he did it vertically and if the angle of descent was 60 degrees and it was measured from the top, that would be 25 centimetres then it was this -- this height was 21.5 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Do not know for sure at this very moment whether, when comparing the measurement of Professor Zecevic, whether we should compare that with 21 centimetres or even the projection of 20 sine centimetres which would bring us even considerably below 20 centimetres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we cannot have the depth one 25 and the other one 20 and then to have a height which is the total height lesser than that. If it's at an angle then this side could be 25 and this 20, then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. But there is at least a question mark here in the measurement of Dr. Zecevic; is that -- do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree on that. Here I have the transcript of his testimony and marked it in red, this part in relation to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't stated precisely how the measurement was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that creates some uncertainty. I take you back to where we calculated that you need a speed of 268 metres per second in order to arrive at the penetration as we found it using your tables as you gave them to us. First of all, would we agree that the value of 268 is quite different from the value of 528 you gave us in your report on page 56?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is in relation to the velocity measured, impact velocity measured for concrete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that it is different, yes, it is different because it's -- this is not concrete, it's logical that there is a difference, we're not talking about concrete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it's not logical, I expect you to be logical and hope that I am logical as well. Two hundred and sixty-eight metres per second, you said that no mortar could fire a projectile such that it would land at a speed of 528 metres per second. Now, if we forget about concrete, and if we talk about two centimetres of asphalt and other centimetres of soil, stones, we are talking about a velocity of 268, would there be a mortar that could fire a projectile that would land at the level 500 metres lower than the level of firing with an arrival speed of 268 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That could be, Your Honour, which is what I said when I gave you this value 268, that was calculated approximately together with the trajectory but yes, it is possible. Of course that the speed goes up and 268 is acceptable, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
