utterances.text: So do I understand that you say that your calculation on page 56 which led you to the conclusion that a mortar could never fire a projectile that would land with the speed you indicated, that if we replace the 528 metres per second by 268 metres per second, and if we take into consideration that the landing speed would be higher because of the difference in altitude between firing level and level of impact, that then a mortar could approximately cause such a velocity at impact? I noticed that you gave as a value 260 as a maximum in your homework, 258 for one trajectory, 260 for the other, that's the homework you did for me and this is plus two or three per cent. Would you also agree with me that if the calculations would give a variation of 10 per cent, that these two values are not, per se, incompatible, that means that the value for the maximum speed of impact at the level 500 metre lower and the velocity you would need for an impact of 20 centimetres, 20 centimetres H and not LP, would you agree with that? Is my reasoning correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, yes, but Your Honours, 268 is for the top end of the angles, we saw that 268 to 248 and 20 extra would come to 268. When we have an angle of descent, 56 degrees, the drop velocity of the shell is 235 metres per second and we add this velocity on it to it and that would be about 258 metres per second you have that in the table, 258. So, 104 metres per second is the difference -- sorry, yeah, yeah, that is the difference as if we take this velocity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we make all these adjustments and if we keep in mind that there is some uncertainty as to the way Professor Zecevic measured diagonally or on the vertical difference between surface, and if we take into consideration that we do not know the exact composition of the soil which would also be able to create perhaps a variation of 10 per cent or even as the Sandia report says up to 100 per cent, would you agree with me that your conclusion just related to this element, I'm not talking about the damage done to the -- I'm just excluding the other elements, of course, you've taken into consideration as well -- would you agree with me that it is not obvious that just on the basis of these ballistic calculation that it's not obvious that the stabiliser did not play any part in the claimed penetration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we have to bear in mind the fact that this surface was covered with a 2 centimetre layer of concrete, that's what Mr. Zecevic said and this can be seen in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just say, yesterday, when shown the photograph, you said that it was clear of -- or from the video, I do not know, you said it was clear, that it was asphalt surface. The testimony of Dr. Zecevic - I just read that out to you - is that it was a layer of asphalt probably two centimetres thick, but of course if it would have been concrete or if -- well, there are a lot of other variables we could think of but I'm just trying to understand whether your expertise with the as you write it obviously exclude for a scenario as we find it in the Prosecution's case? That's what I'm trying to establish. And of course there are still a lot of uncertainties, we do not know exactly what the soil was we do not know exactly how thick the layer of asphalt was, we do not know exactly how Dr. Zecevic measured the depth if he did it diagonally, it might considerably change. We do not know exactly what the impact would be according to the American report, what deviation it would give, 20 per cent, 10 per cent, 5 per cent, 100 per cent, but you told us before that it would make no difference whatsoever to your conclusion whether 100 per cent deviation in the values assumed would occur. I have some difficulties in understanding this when I see that you confirmed that a projectile could land under the circumstances given, at a speed of 260 metres per second and you would need 268 metres per second to achieve the penetration. So I have some difficulties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, with regard to the 100 per cent deviation, I said that that related to the calculations based on the Sandia laboratory formulations. If we increased these results by 100 per cent, our conclusion would still be the same because it's a far lower value than what is in the report on what the measurements in the report on the length of penetration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And if you would reduce them by 100 per cent they say that there's imprecision up to 100 per cent it could be more, it could be less, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of these firing tables, the depth of penetration of the stabiliser calculated on the basis of the Sandia method, the penetration depth ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you looking for the comparative table of stabilisers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the comparative table for stabilisers. I have the Serbian version here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it true that there are no values known for the laboratory you're just referring to because I see six arrows saying, "Not calculated for penetration in macadam."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Macadam isn't included here. We just did this for concrete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we don't know it for macadam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the data we at the time, no macadam was mentioned there. Soil was mentioned and various types of soil, soil with little stones, soil which had sand in it and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you have this table in front of you before I -- we continue, I'd like to ask you one further question. You have told us several times that by using the Berezin formula, you used the most favorable approach, and I did understand favorable for the Prosecution's case. May I ask you to compare for macadam the values calculated according to the Berezin formula and according to the Gabeaud formula for macadam. I'm just asking you to compare these two. Am I correct when I read that from the six figures given for macadam, that Gabeaud gives higher values in five out of six?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For greater angles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, greater. All the figures given for macadam and comparing the Berezin and the Gabeaud, I see that Gabeaud, to speak in your terms, gives, on five out of six situations, a more favorable outcome for the Prosecution's case, that is, more penetration at the same speed of impact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in terms of the numbers, yes, but the Gabeaud method is a method established at the beginning of the 20th century and the Sutterlin method was based on the most recent research in the 60s carried out in France. So when I said that, that was in relation to Sutterlin and Young and Berezin's method was far less favorable but we excluded Gabeaud because his method was at the end of the 19th and beginning of 20th century.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will stop you there. I come back to that in a second. Do you agree with me that where you presented different methods of calculation that Berezin not in all situations gives the most favorable outcome for the Prosecution's case on the basis of these figures you presented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to contemporary methods, it gives less favorable methods. Sutterlin and Young were the main methods and that's what Zecevic referred to, that's why we introduced this. Gabeaud's method is an old one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Berezin is even older as far as I see on the -- let me put one more question to you what exactly explains the huge differences in the different systems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how this is determined depends on the methodology. They all started from one methodology, Jacob Dema [phoen]. In fact it was done on the basis of penetrating armour and then these methods were modified and on the basis of experiments, they determined the co-efficients for soil of this kind. I have a table here of all the possible values for each method in question and that alone provides an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that the values are quite different. And you said it's a matter of methodology, I'll not put at this moment to you what exactly the difference in the methodology is. Would the most recent, what you refer to as Young SNL USA 1997, what in the methodology makes that -- the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More favorable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- no, let me put the question differently to you. These methodologies, would they generally result in a higher outcome or a lower outcome according to the material --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The new methods give lower values, the values that they arrive at are significantly lower. Your Honour, with regard to the mistake we made, M 015 we took 0.46 times N.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- did you make a mistake in this table or were you referring to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm returning to that formula, you know, where we made a mistake. We made a mistake with regard to the length of penetration. We got a depth of penetration that was twice as great than if we had taken the right coefficient because 048 times 04 equals 0.7, if you multiply this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want to concentrate now on this table rather than seeing what the consequences would be for the mistake you made. I see that you said the newest methodology would give a lower outcome. When I compare Gabeaud with Young, then I see that generally, Young, although newer, has a higher outcome than the old Gabeaud. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for concrete surfaces, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no figures for macadam as far as Young is concerned. So the -- your testimony I just heard that the new methodology brings lower outcomes is not generally true but is, for example, true when you compare Berezin to Young but would not be true if you compare Gabeaud with Berezin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, the problem has to do with the resistance than is say with concrete. 19th century and 20th or 21st century concrete. These -- various times are concrete are quite different. When you are examining the resistance of concrete, you're not examining the resistance of concrete in a street or the resistance of a building's concrete, you are examining the resistance of reinforced concrete, concrete used in bunkers or in shelters and the concrete used for these structures is far better and so you get a lower values for the penetration of certain projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Do I understand you well that your testimony is that if you do not have detailed knowledge of exactly the composition of the surface and the layers below the surface, that it would be very difficult to draw conclusions with a sufficient level of certainty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If the quality of the ground is better than the -- what we assumed, the calculations as you can see were made, greater length of penetration were obtained only in marsh land. You could see that in the tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all of this raises three problems. The first one is can the Defence have a copy of your scheme, of your sketch the first one shown on the screen which shows an elevation point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be marked for identification. It was just based on assumptions that seem to come close to what the Prosecution alleges has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second problem is that the time that your Trial Chamber has taken and it appears it's benefited the Prosecution to a great extent, it hasn't benefited us much, it means that we will have very little time or not enough time. And the third matter that I would like to raise, Mr. President, is -- and for two reasons, is as follows: We haven't asked this witness about the difference of altitude in relation to the highest elevation held by the Muslim forces above Markale and I think that it would have been absolutely necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are just theoretically looking at what a difference would be at 500 metres. If the Prosecution thinks it came from Mrkovici which has been said several times, at least from the direction of Mrkovici, I think that does not establish in whatever way, where it came from Mrkovici, you -- in order to draw whatever conclusion you should know at least what would be the level of the Markale market in order to calculate any difference so that's -- but we are talking now with an expert witness which I do not expect to have established facts which are not specifically within his field of expertise. So I would agree that if someone would like to draw conclusions from it, that you would need to know more and apart from that, the Chamber has decided that this is a very important expert witness. As I told you before, the Chamber would have some questions and since it came up it was related directly to what the witness was asked about, that was the reason why I sought to clarify things, not in the benefit of the Prosecution, not in the benefit of the Defence, but, as I hope, in the benefit of the search for the truth. Therefore, if there would be no more time needed, we might not finish with this expert witness today, but that, of course, creates another problem. Professor Vilicic, if we would not be able to get all the answers we would like to have today, would you still be available next Monday to finish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, yes, but can I just say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the direction of 18 degrees with relation to the north, up to Mrkovici you don't have a single elevation which is higher than 1.000 metres. Markale is at an altitude of about 600 metres above sea level so we don't have an altitude of 500 metres above sea level, not in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... No one asks you to know exactly what the levels are. I take it that your expertise is not mainly on saying that the Eiffel tower is 300 metres high although you might measure it but you didn't do it and I think the questions put to you did not ask from you exactly how high what hills were around Sarajevo neither what would be the level of the city of the Sarajevo so so you say I do not know whether there could be a level difference of 500 metre exist in the area. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that I expressed myself badly and what I would like to say is the following: In order for you to be able to ask questions about the residual velocity before impact, on a lower point, you asked the witness to make calculations regarding a difference of 500 metres. And unfortunately the Defence is not in a position to do these calculations for other distances. What we do know is that there were Muslim positions which were at an altitude and as a result if these calculations aren't made by the witness, since we can't contact him, we are handicapped and I'm saying this because if we had regarded the position of the Prosecution we would also have had to take into consideration the highest possible elevation of the so-called Muslim forces and then carry out these calculations to obtain the results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would have listened well, when I asked the witness to do the homework, I asked, as a matter of fact, calculations, steps of 100 metres higher and lower. Even made a small sketch there where you find both firing uphill as firing downhill. The expert witness presented 500 metres downhill where I asked for 100 -- so that's what we got and therefore on the basis of that, I put the questions to him. But certainly there will be a way even if the parties would sit together and say could we ask someone who knows about this, could calculate for us the different levels there would be of course this or -- I don't think that there should be any problem that if it's of importance for the Defence to calculate that. There might be 500 metres difference in level for Muslim positions as well. I do not even know if there is a 500 metres difference level for Serb positions. I do not know. It's up to the parties to establish the necessary facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President, but I just like to say that I doubt that I'll find a professor of mathematics over the weekend who has the same competence of Mr. Vilicic, someone who could help me to make these calculations but I will try to find one or two experts over the weekend to help me do this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps once Professor Vilicic has finished his testimony in this Court where he said that he has a little instrument that allows him very well to make the precise calculations, that perhaps then afterwards he could be of assistance. Mr. Stamp, we'll follow the same procedure that questions put by the Bench were not calculated for the Defence nor will they be calculated for the Prosecution unless, Mr. Stamp, you would say that it is a time for the break and then we'll have a break until quarter to one. Yes. Then we'll adjourn until a quarter to one. --- Break taken at 12:25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor, you stated that the maximum -- and that is at page 54 of your report, you stated that the maximum theoretical speed of tail stabiliser throwing is 154 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Didn't Dr. Vukasinovic in his published work presented to the symposium of the military institute of the JNA go -- and this is in 1997, go further to do a more precise calculation of the maximum speed of stabiliser throwing?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the latest calculation. He did this personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see his paper that he presented in respect to this matter with all the charts, graphs or calculations or -- I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so that there is no confusion, in relation to the way the question was phrased on page 57 at the end, speaking about the maximum theoretical speed of the stabiliser, what I would like is could the Prosecution clarify this, can they be more precise? Can they just say where this is indicated on page 54 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness responded yes, but Mr. Stamp, your question was that the witness stated that the maximum theoretical speed of tail stabiliser throwing is 154 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think I referred to page 54 of the report in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you refer to the speed or at least to say the negative speed or the deceleration of a tail fin upon explosion of a mortar because that's what I find on page 54. And that's not exactly the same as the maximum speed. It's by which speed a tail fin -- the speed of a tail fin will be reduced by the detonation results; is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And it is referred to in the report as a maximum theoretical speed of tail stabiliser throwing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Throwing, yes. Yes. Where do we find exactly this term because it's a bit unclear to me, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No, it's not true, Mr. Stamp, you're making a mistake. The sentence before the equation is, "In order that a stabiliser can penetrate to the depth of it shall possess the minimum impact speed which is the sum of the speed obtained by solving the said equation for calculating" -- no, no, I do agree. You're right. I have to apologise, it's the second part of the equation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In Dr. Vukasinovic's work, did he say that the maximal theoretical velocity at which a stabiliser is propeled backward is the same, 154 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, to tell the truth, but this calculation, what's in the report, this was done Vukasinovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. I suggest to you that Dr. Vukasinovic in his published work went on to do a more precise calculation of the speed of the throwback and concluded that on the basis of a numerical assimilations, the velocity of the stabiliser body at the end of the process of expulsive propulsion is 140.5 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1997, at that time, Vukasinovic was not a doctor, he was doing his Ph.D thesis and he conducted a bunch of experiments and what you see in the report is his very last research work with was from his Ph.D, checked with dozens of experiments. What you have is you have data from his published work which is 145 metres but Zecevic himself spoke that there could be different values depending on which author is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it states very clearly in the report that it was Vukasinovic himself who conducted this analysis. He is number three on this list and he is also somebody who did this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Is about 14 [Realtime transcript read in error "40"] metres per second higher than the figure that he gives in his published work; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript reads 40 metres whereas I take it that you said 14 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 14 metres.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you also want to discredit and disqualify Dr. Vukasinovic, saying this value is not the right one that he said here. This is the correct value. This is the correct value acquired and published in the Ph.D thesis of Dr. Vukasinovic. Vukasinovic did this on the basis of much more precise data of detonation speed and the materials that are used and according to this formula as you can see, the main parameter which influences this speed is detonation speed of the explosive, depending on what was used as the charge the projectile and here he used for 6.870 metres he used detonation speed that was measured and he came himself to this conclusion that the speed was 154 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well with your leave, Mr. President, and with the assistance of the usher could I show to the witness a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, is this a standard slow motion -- well, is the section on the right a standard photograph of the fragments obtained from the explosion of a mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a picture of the fragments of an 82 millimetre shell from the prospects of the federal administration, from the brochures for an enterprise that is involved in special production of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the fragmentation, witness, could you -- Professor, please, the fragmentation of the 82 millimetre mortar shell is substantially the same in respect to the shape of the fragments as the 120 millimetre mortar shell; do you agree? Yes, I see you have the same photograph, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, in principle, generally speaking, you can also make this kind of photograph for the 120 millimetre shell it's a question of the size of fragments but there is a difference depending on the coefficient of charge so-called, also the quality of the steel, the material, and if I may say, I know that there was the MA that is done. Fehmia Shahir [phoen] has conducted this work on recommendation upon Stamatovic and myself and he did a master's thesis regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. And to the left of the photograph, you see at the top the fragment shards that would emanate from the side of the shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the evidence that the material is poor, that the quality of the material that the shell is made of is poor. If you are asking my opinion, this is a very poor way that a shell has fragmented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you notice that in the -- on the left below there are fragments, chunkier fragments, if I could use that expression, indicating the particles from the front ogival part of the shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't confirm that on such a poor photograph, not according to the form, you couldn't even say that it comes -- originates from the frontal part. That's a very provisional assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you see the chunkier-looking shells in the centre of the photograph to the right? Sorry, not chunkier-looking shells but chunkier-looking fragments?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean these fragments here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, photograph of the --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these fragments here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean that this was a photograph that was made on the basis of the fragmentation in length of the shell? You mean that it goes from the centre to the periphery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that it goes from the centre. I'm just asking whether --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are standard-size fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you remove that, please? This photograph or a document containing two photographs of cross sections of a mortar fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The top photograph shows a cross-section of the UTU-M78 fuse which uses both the 120 and 82 millimetre mortar shells and the bottom photograph shows the UTU-M78 fuse binding and the M62 P3 120 metre shell front ogival part. I understand you have those photographs. But look at the photograph. And look at the bottom one.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only fuse UTU-M78.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Both of them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Both of those are views of UTU-M78.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that within the fuse, there are several subsystems which are connected by screw fittings of different sizes so there are different thread sizing for circular subsystems within the fuse?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation is not correct. Not correct. [Interpretation] The thread, he said the thread is different, yes, there are different threads, yes [In English] There is different filetage exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will express to you that during the explosion process, because the jacket of a shell and also the fuse stretches before it explodes, all of these parts are distorted.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could that photograph be removed. Could the witness be shown this document with your leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for something? Can we have that photograph back so that you can see that there is no reductor on that shell?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We agree that there are sometimes reductors used and sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do agree. You want to point out to us that there is no reductor on the photograph, that is not in dis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very precisely, the fuse UTU-M78 when it is used for 120 millimetre mortar shell does not have the reductor because diameter of the hole of the opening is large enough. It is only used for the fuse UTU --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just stop you there seems to be no disagreement on that, so thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just -- I have shown you that document because I want to understand what you were explaining to us about the tests that were done and again, I think I've given up all the documents and not retained a copy. Is there a spare copy? Thank you. Do you see on that document if you --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I told you yesterday that the checking of the fuse safety is done by horizontal firing on to an obstacle in which it's not supposed to be hit with. It's a check for the safety. It's at that distance when you fire a mortar, for instance, through the forest, when the -- during the projectile of the trajectory this should not hit the branches and become activated because otherwise the crew that is firing the mortar would get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, yes. And also tests the fuse for instantaneous action and delayed action.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both. Please, obviously I have to explain the function of the fuse in this sense. The fuse, even set for instantaneous and with a time-delay function must have safety at the barrel so that it doesn't explode when it leaves the barrel. That's why it's been checked, five of them for the time delay -- for the instantaneous and then five for the time delay, that's been checked and that's for a barrel that's been placed to fire horizontally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, and this document indicates that the fuses are also checked for the instantaneous action and the delayed action?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, safety in front of the barrel so that it doesn't explode at the certain distance away from the muzzle because at that moment, the elements that can initiate the explosion of the shell are not yet in the -- they haven't left the safety position. They later come into the safety position that would enable them for when the shell hit a hard obstacle then explosion would occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do these protocols also indicate that the shells -- sorry, the fuses are checked to see whether or not they activate instantaneously if checked on instantaneous action and with the delayed effect if set on delayed action?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This protocol, you mean this protocol? This protocol is only checking for the safety of the fuse in front of the muzzle as it leaves the muzzle and even some fuses have been vibrated and then they are mounted and then this is checking for transport conditions when ammunition and fuses are being transported and shaken so what is done to ensure the safety that after this period of shaking when they are then -- when they are placed upon the shells that they do not explode. That's arming so it's the fuse that arms the weapon, that arms the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But would you agree with me that the fuses are checked to see whether or not they activate before penetrating a board one-inch thick when the impact velocity is 121 metres per second and I'm not suggesting that that arises from the protocol but that is as far as you understand that the instantaneous action of the fuse?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you haven't understood this issue at all. This is the velocity for O plus one charge, first increment charge why is this checked? Because this is the minimal speed at which the mortar fires. These are also minimum accelerations. With minimum accelerations, we check whether the fuse function is safe. It has nothing to do with 101 metre per second drop velocity. These are two completely separate issues. This is just a muzzle velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Could you take away the document, please. What I'm asking you now and this is an issue that you know that the tests are for the instant action of a fuse the criteria is whether or not at 121 metres per second it will explode before it penetrates a board one-inch thick?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not 121 metres if you are talking about the criteria it's a bit greater, 117 to 123, that's what the velocity is said to be of each shell -- for each shell to be accepted -- to accept that the fuse has been tested and to accept that it's correct. If there's an explosion at 121 then it means that that series of fuses doesn't correspond to the standards that are used and then it is sent back for re-examination. This is the form of the fuse that is accepted it has nothing to do with sensitivity in the field, this is the safety that you need at the muzzle of the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, doctor, one minute. You have told us that they have tests to see whether or not the fuse activates and is the standard for passing a fuse as instantaneous whether or not it activates before it passes through a wooden board one-inch thick when fired at 117 to 1 -- when approaching at an impact velocity of 117 to 121 metres per second standard that is what is used in the test.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious that you don't understand what the problem is. From 120 metres at a certain distance we penetrate a board without the fuse reacting but if we'd someplace a screen at 10 metres from that screen then the shell should explode. In other words, you are correct when you say that 120 metres is the velocity at which you check the safety and the muzzle barrel and the safety of the fuse and the time-delayed fuse so this test is one to check the quality of the fuse or rather to check that safety is adequate in the muzzle of the barrel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere and see whether I can take away whatever confusion. Professor Vilicic, I do understand that you and Mr. Stamp agree on what is the criteria, what is the value on which a fuse should activate and that this report is a test that, at this speed, with this thick plank, it would not yet activate if it's placed so close to the barrel, it should only activate if that plank would be at a further distance from the barrel and therefore, the report says no fuse acted on impact with the obstacle or immediately behind it because it should not act at this short distance. Is that a correct understanding? I hope it assists you Mr. Stamp, I don't know, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, to some degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So we understand that. Now, separate and apart from that document, and the issue of fuse safety, there are also quite different tests that are used to check the -- whether or not the fuses will react instantaneously and that test really is whether or not the fuse reacts before penetrating a board of one-inch thick.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not at this distance that we have here. This is positive because it didn't react at a greater distance it has to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, do you know of any published scientific work in respect to the 82 millimetre mortar tail fin remaining on the scene, the impact site, and could you give us a reference so we could check it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I ask for some more information because I don't think it's clear. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question is -- but please correct me, Mr. Stamp, is whether you know of any publication which refers to a 82 millimetre mortar tail fin remaining on the site of the impact, not embedded or embedded or not embedded, Mr. Stamp, or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Embedded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question is whether you know of any publication of a 82 mortar tail fin after the explosion found embedded in the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you give us a reference so we can check it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, there are so many works, but they're not often accessible but from all our conclusions, yes, a stabiliser of an 82 millimetre can remain in place under certain conditions. If the velocity is 190 metres it will he remain but if it's 80 it will be ejected in the direction which is opposite to the direction from which it came. In the case of 82 millimetre and 120 millimetre shells, we have various factors given the small mass of the stabiliser, the performance is quite different, it can't lodge in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you objecting, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the transcript it was very fast. I'm not sure that I understood correctly, 190 and 80 on the other hand, it was at page 69, line 4, I don't know if there was a mistake but it was going very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 70 metres, instead of 80 because it's muzzle velocity of basis charge for mortar bombs of 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that the dynamics are the same but the values are different from those calculated in respect of 120 millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to make some propositions to you which I will call suggestions. If you agree with me, say yes. If you disagree with me, say no. I suggest to you that the propellant used -- I beg your pardon, the explosive used in the 82 millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The gunpowder, because it is IDX [phoen] or a mixture of TNT or CH-50 it has a greater push on the stabiliser fin of a 82 millimetre mortar than a 120 millimetre mortar, would you agree with that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President -- no, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the explosive charge is such then it has a greater velocity than if all that is used is TNT. It's a mixture a 50/50 mixture of TNT and CH-50. This is used with the last models of shells that were produced after the conflict in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I told you, Doctor, just answer me yes, if you agree and no, if you don't and you have given that information at page 3 of your report. At table 9 of your report, and that's on page 9, you show the values of the velocity of the fragments on the detonation of a shell and you notice that because of this different type of explosive, the speed for the 182 [sic] millimetre fragments is 109 metres per second faster than the 120 millimetre fragments?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would be grateful if Mr. Stamp could slow down, we're told about page 3 table 9 and Ms. Pilipovic has to check in the text and none of these references seem to correspond what I can see. Let's mention which pages and which tables we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I have some difficulties in finding table 9 on page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Table 4, page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Table 5, table 5, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the English report, it's table 4 at page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The velocity of the fragments do I see them -- yes, I see them that's for fragments dispersions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes it's 109 metres per second faster than the 82 millimetre shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at some of the drawings that you did or that you reproduced from other published work at page 12? Look at figure 2.1 and 2.2 -- sorry, I beg your pardon, figure --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, Mr. President, we don't have the references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp was about to correct himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Figure 2.12 at page 11 and figure 2.13 at page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in the dynamics at the explosion and Dr. Vukasinovic has proven that in the dynamics of the explosion of the 82 millimetre shell as compared to the 120 millimetre mortar shell a greater proportion of the fragments are pushed backwards in the 82 millimetre than in the 120 millimetre, would you agree with that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can there be a greater number of fragments since the case of the shell is four times lighter than that of 120 millimetre shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I didn't say a greater number. I said a greater proportion of the fragments of the 82 millimetre mortar shell is pushed backwards than for the 120 millimetre and that is clear from Dr. Vukasinovic's work. Do you agree? Do you agree, yes or no, doctor, please, let's move quickly.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The velocity is greater, the fragments of the same mass will go further, that is what is correct because if the projectile has CH-50, its velocity of the fragments is greater than for that of 120 millimetre shell which is filled with TNT.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you that not only is the velocity pushing it backward much faster but the proportion, proportion of the fragments going backward is also much higher than in the 122 millimetre shell, agree or disagree. If you agree please say yes, if you don't, please say no.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. It's not the same value.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the speed of stabiliser detachment in the 82 millimetre mortar is much faster than its maximum impact velocity of 194 metres per second and therefore, unless it is stopped by an obstacle, it never remains at the site of the explosion. It is always blown back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise but what is the maximum velocity of 194, 194?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Decisive issue. The question to you, Professor Vilicic, is whether the back-pushing power of the explosion in an 82 millimetre mortar would always be such that it is higher, that it causes a higher velocity backwards than the velocity of the tail fin at that moment and therefore, it cannot ever land embedded in the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does not become embedded in the ground. It remains where the crater is located. It never becomes embedded not because the ejection speed is great, but because the mass of the stabiliser is fairly small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I therefore -- following from that, I suggest to you that all of your conclusions that you have made in your study in respect to the absence of the 82 millimetre stabiliser fin have no foundation in scientific research because it is always blown back unless stopped by an object. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That's not correct. That is totally wrong. You have information that is totally wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your report in respect to incident 4, it is suggested that you improperly used a close-up photograph of a lodged stabiliser fin to determine angle of descent when you, as a scientist, know that you can use the fragment traces on the ground to come to an accurate assessment of angle of descent and you have done it in respect to the Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that you are constantly referring to me, trying to discredit me as a scientist and secondly have a look at the photograph of the 120 millimetre shell that hit the path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Vilicic, you are not to comment on the approach of the Prosecution. The Prosecution may test your report, they may put questions to you. At the end of your testimony, I'll give you an opportunity, the Chamber will give you an opportunity to explain whatever your thought was unexplained of course within certain limits as far as time is concerned so therefore, you have the an opportunity but the Prosecution is under time restraint and therefore, they are allowed to ask you just to say whether you agree or disagree with the certain position taken by the Prosecution. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to know is whether Mr. Stamp was referring to -- with regard to what he calls the close-up photograph, I think that those are the terms that he used. Is he referring to the photograph that we have on page 45 or is he referring to some other photograph in relation to the stabiliser because I'm afraid that I'm not following this. That's my only question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at the report by the witness which was tendered on -- which the Defence intend to tender, it's their production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was just on the ELMO, I think the photograph you referred to. Could you please put it back what you just had on the ELMO, is that the photograph you are referring to, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. Could we quickly get exhibit 2245 -- 2247.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Vilicic, would you please let the usher put the photographs on the screen. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Photograph 00268248.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think this should be the photograph you're referring to, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while waiting, I think that the bell has rung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Quite clearly at the beginning of the session that we cannot sit any longer than quarter to 2.00 so you may finish this question and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Witness, that you can never use a close-up photograph to judge angle of descent and to conclude that it is approximately 90 degrees when you yourself know of and have used more scientific procedures to determine angle of descent. Yes or no? Yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One suggestion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said that was your last question and I keep to that, stick to that. If there is really an issue that should be raised, we'll see whether the Chamber would be willing to grant leave but as it stands now, same time for you as for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, as it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Vilicic, we will adjourn for the day. We have not yet finished your examination so we'd like to see you back in this Court next Monday in the afternoon, that is, at a quarter past 2.00. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given and you are still about to give. We'll adjourn until Monday at quarter past 2.00.
